newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire enters critical week as rebels vow final assault.
newsitem.headline: Zaire enters critical week as rebels vow final assault.

text.p: Zaire's civil war entered a critical week with world attention focused on whether South African mediation could save the capital Kinshasa from encroaching rebels.

A delicate search for a peaceful resolution of the six-month-old conflict looked all the more elusive with rebel leader Laurent Kabila's explosive declaration that he was building up forces for a final move on Kinshasa.
Official South African sources said last week that much-expected talks between Kabila and the man he wants to topple, President Mobutu Sese Seko, might be held on Wednesday.
But there was no firm sign by Sunday that the meeting was about to take place imminently in South Africa or anywhere else.
Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nganza Mobutu, would not give any precise indication of what to expect. "The two teams are still working out the details," he told Reuters by telephone.

Kabila insists that a meeting, if it takes place, will be a only formal setting for Mobutu to hand over the power he has held for 32 years. Mobutu's camp say talks should lead to elections to enable the people to decide if they still want him.
There was further disquiet in Kinshasa when a scheduled visit by Benin's President Mathieu Kerekou was called off at the last minute on Sunday without official explantion.
A restricted party of international reporters was cleared to cover Kerekou's meeting with Mobutu and a red-carpet reception had been set before news came that he was no longer coming.

Kerekou has not been linked to diplomatic peace efforts over Zaire. But as a military strongman who lost power and regained it through elections, he would be qualified to advise Mobutu to step aside gracefully, political analysts said.
Given Mobutu's failing health, the abrupt cancellation of such a high-level schedule was bound to raise speculation about his condition.
The 66-year-old leader had cancer surgery last August and is still receiving treatment, although he looked in fair shape in his last public appearance only days ago.
The uncertainty and fears that Kinshasa could be cut off from Zaire's only seaport propmted a search for alternative shipping routes.

Bankers said importers might shift trade from the Atlantic port of Matadi to neighbouring Congo. "At least one shipper is already doing it and others are considering doing so as well," said a Kinshasa-based banker.

Kabila said he had recruited 100,000 new guerrillas and was ready to open a fresh war front from Bas Zaire (Lower Zaire) province, which includes Matadi, site of Zaire's lifeblood oil refinery and gateway for most imported goods.
Bankers and traders said conditions in Kinshasa could deteriorate rapidly if vital supply routes were cut.
Importers have run down stocks of food and other products for months for fear of looting by Zaire's poorly paid and ill-disciplined army, business and public sector sources say.
Kabila says his forces, who have overrun about half of the vast Central African country including its richest mining provinces, will be in Kinshasa in three weeks.

Diplomats and military analysts place them within 500 km (300 miles) of Kinshasa and say Kabila is building up troops and weaponry in the city of Kananga 600 km (370 miles) away in preparation for an advance from the east.
